source.title: Overfitting Can Be Harmless for Basis Pursuit, But Only to a Degree
source.authors: Pei-Zhong Ju; Xiao-Jun Lin; Jia Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent in a different setting and with a different model class: analytical bounds and numerical sweeps for overfitting Basis Pursuit in sparse Gaussian linear regression, rather than deep networks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own analytical bounds and numerical model-error sweeps. It discusses the minimum-ℓ2-norm solution, but the cited Eq. (11) comparison is not extracted as a separate result. Numerical plot values are not given in the text, so those rows record figure-only values.
record.test_reason: The study derives its own finite-n, finite-p bounds and runs its own simulations of model error versus p for overfitting Basis Pursuit in sparse Gaussian linear regression. This is a non-deep model class, and it directly tests whether error falls again past p = n (V4). Its own Fig. 2 and Eq. (9) also show more samples raising error at fixed p in the overparameterized region (V3).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that, for sparse linear models with i.i.d. Gaussian features, overfitting BP shows double descent: its model-error upper bound decreases with p up to a limit exponential in n. That bound is independent of signal strength, and for high SNR and sparse models BP's descent floor is lower and wider than min-ℓ2's. They add that error eventually rises again at very large p. Overfitting solutions also cannot reach the error of well-tuned LASSO.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses ℓ1-minimizing Basis Pursuit on sparse Gaussian linear regression, not deep-network size scaling; it combines finite-parameter analytical bounds and numerical simulations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior depends on p and on the regime: error descends beyond n but rises again for very large p. The numerical comparisons also vary n, sparsity s, signal strength ||β||₂, and noise norm ||ε_train||₂.

fits_no_version.finding: In the descent region, the scaled error n^(-1/4)||w_BP||₂ levels off for large n. It is nearly unchanged between s = 1 and s = 20, and about 4× higher when ||ε_train||₂ rises from 0.15 to 0.6 (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the overparameterized descent region, interpolating-solution error scales with noise level and sample size but not with sparsity or signal strength.

fits_no_version.finding: BP's descent in the overfitting region does not vary much with signal strength ||β||₂, unlike min-ℓ2 solutions (Fig. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The height of the second descent depends on the interpolating norm: ℓ1 interpolation avoids the signal 'spill' that min-ℓ2 shows.

record.problems: The main theoretical result is an upper bound rather than an exact risk characterization; the authors note loose constants and a gap between their upper and lower bounds. Numerical values are presented in plots without numerical table entries. The setting is sparse Gaussian linear regression and does not establish behavior in deep networks or other feature distributions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results omitted. Eq. (11)'s min-ℓ2 comparison is presented as a comparison based on prior work, not extracted as an independent study result.

untested.parts: Sample-size effect shown only at fixed p inside the overparameterized descent region, not as a sample-wise peak at the interpolation threshold.
Only BP (and a min-ℓ2 comparator) with isotropic Gaussian features; other model classes and feature models are untested.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.

Error scales with noise norm in the descent region, but the study does not test whether noise drives the peak. It reports no multiple peaks and does not tune regularization to see whether the peak disappears; LASSO is only discussed from the literature.

missing.what: The study's own simulated min-ℓ2-norm interpolation curves. They show a second descent past p = n that quickly returns to the null risk, varies with ||β||₂, and has a narrower, higher floor than BP.
missing.locator: Figure 1 (dashed curves) and discussion items (i), (ii) and (iv) in Section 3

missing.what: A lower bound showing BP's descent can be no faster than 1/sqrt(ln p), so the second descent is slow in p.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Plotted values are figure-only. The p < n branch of the curves is the min-MSE solution, not BP, so the peak itself comes from least squares. The V3 evidence concerns increasing n at fixed overparameterized p, not a sample-wise peak at n ≈ p.

versions.untested_parts: No deep-network experiment; the tested system is sparse linear regression with Basis Pursuit.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No direct test of increasing sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests Basis Pursuit in sparse Gaussian linear regression, not a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across size, epochs, and samples.

The study varies noise magnitude in a model-error plot and discusses regularized LASSO, but does not test whether noise drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters or test of whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shape.

rows.subject: Basis Pursuit (BP)
rows.operation_detail: Analytical bound on model error as p increases in the overparameterized regime.
rows.baseline: At p = n, BP coincides with the min-MSE solution with high probability; the text states that the min-MSE model error peaks near p = n.
rows.note: This is an upper bound, not an exact risk curve. The authors interpret it as showing a decreasing-error region past the peak.
rows.check: Eq. (9) is an upper bound that decreases in p, not the error itself, so partial is right for V4. The bound also grows with n (the (7n/ln p)^(1/4) term), which the authors read as larger n worsening BP error at fixed p (V3).

source_check.correct: The sparsity condition is s ≤ sqrt(n/[7168 ln(16n)]). The feature range is (16n)^4 ≤ p ≤ exp(n/(1792s²)).
source_check.locator_found: Section 3, Theorem 2, Eq. (9); Appendix F, Eqs. (40)–(42).
source_check.problem: The condition omits the square root in the sparsity bound and misstates the lower endpoint of the p interval.

relationships.reason: The Eq. (9) upper bound decreases with p (r1), and the simulations show a peak at p = n followed by a second descent for n = 150 to 600 (r3–r8).
relationships.display_finding: A risk upper bound decreased with p, while simulations with n from 150 to 600 showed a peak at p=n followed by a second descent.
